comparison: Perfect alignment on personalization methodology (C33, C114, C115). Both recognize the individualized stimulation approach as a strength. OpenEval notes the claim about reducing variability (C115) is somewhat speculative since no direct comparison was made, while peer reviewers explicitly praised this as optimizing signal-to-noise ratio without questioning the interpretation.

Strong agreement on clinical translation claims (C11, C85, C145-C149). Both appropriately recognize these as speculative future applications. OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN emphasizing lack of direct evidence in patient populations, while peer reviewers rate as SUPPORTED but explicitly acknowledge these require further validation and are appropriately hedged.

High concordance on connectivity findings (C67-C75, C9, C107). Both accept the PC-hippocampus connectivity increases with appropriate statistical corrections. OpenEval provides detailed technical validation of ROI and seed-to-voxel analyses, while peer reviewers explicitly affirmed the connectivity evidence and praised the mechanistic experiments.

Strong agreement on gamma oscillation findings (C59-C65, C8, C102). Both accept the neurophysiological evidence for increased gamma after dual stimulation. OpenEval validates statistical corrections and spatial specificity, while peer reviewers explicitly stated authors 'provide evidence that dual stimulation increased gamma oscillations' and praised the mechanistic experiments.

Agreement on white matter correlation findings (C76-C79, C111, C113). Both accept the MdLF integrity correlation with connectivity changes. OpenEval notes this is correlational not causal and mentions sample size considerations, while peer reviewers acknowledged the structure-function relationship without raising concerns about interpretation.

Both support behavioral memory enhancement findings (C5-C7, C80-C82). OpenEval R6 covers summary claims while peer R1 includes detailed statistical claims (C38-C39, C41-C43, C52, C54-C56). Both recognize convergent evidence across experiments with replication. Peer reviewers explicitly praised methodological quality and replication, while OpenEval validated statistical rigor.

Partial overlap on Experiment 1 behavioral findings. OpenEval R1 covers comprehensive experimental design and statistics (C3, C32-C49), while peer R1 focuses on subset of behavioral outcomes (C38-C39, C41-C43). Both strongly support the findings with OpenEval providing detailed statistical validation and peer reviewers affirming 'solid methods and evidence.'

Partial overlap on Experiment 2 replication. OpenEval R2 addresses replication study (C50-C57) noting smaller sample and limited controls as minor limitations, while peer R1 includes subset of these claims (C52, C54-C56) and explicitly commended the conceptual replication as increasing confidence in results.

Partial overlap on safety and tolerability. OpenEval R1 includes experimental design claims (C3, C32, C36-C37) as part of comprehensive validation, while peer R7 specifically highlights the brief intervention duration and tolerability. Both support these aspects without concerns.

Agreement on negative control findings (C45, C83). OpenEval R8 validates that iTBS alone showed no difference from sham, while peer R2 implicitly accepts these through praise of methodological quality and within-subject design. Both recognize importance of negative findings for establishing combination necessity.

Agreement on short-term memory specificity (C47, C57, C93). OpenEval R10 validates no effects on STMB with appropriate literature context (C94-C95), while peer R2 accepts these negative findings through overall methodological endorsement. Both recognize this establishes intervention specificity.

Agreement on study limitations (C132-C133, C138-C139). OpenEval R14 validates these as reasonable limitations given methodological constraints, while peer R10 accepts them as not undermining main findings. Both recognize these are appropriate acknowledgments that don't constitute serious flaws.

Partial agreement on mechanistic interpretation (C10, C84, C106, C124-C125, C127). OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED but notes these are plausible interpretations going beyond direct demonstration, while peer reviewers explicitly accepted the theta-gamma coupling mechanism and praised the theoretical framework without challenging the proposed mechanism.

Overlap on mechanistic summary claims linking gamma to memory (C8, C102). OpenEval R7 groups these with broader mechanistic interpretations noting some speculation, while peer R3 explicitly affirms the gamma oscillation evidence. Both ultimately support but OpenEval more cautious about causal claims.

Overlap on mechanistic summary for connectivity (C9, C107). OpenEval R7 includes these in mechanistic interpretations with caution about going beyond direct demonstration, while peer R4 explicitly affirms connectivity evidence. Both support but OpenEval emphasizes interpretive nature.

Agreement on spatial specificity (C61). OpenEval R11 validates control region analysis showing spatial specificity (C61, C88-C89), while peer R3 implicitly accepts through praise of methodological quality. Both recognize this strengthens targeted stimulation interpretation.

Partial overlap on mechanistic hypothesis (C124-C125, C127). OpenEval R13 provides detailed validation of tACS-iTBS synergy mechanism with literature support but notes it remains proposed rather than definitively proven, while peer R8 accepts the theta-gamma coupling rationale. Both support the theoretical framework.

Minimal overlap on interpretive integration (C111, C113). OpenEval R18 covers broad interpretive claims integrating findings with literature, noting some speculation about precise mechanisms, while peer R5 specifically addresses structure-function relationship. Both support with appropriate caveats.

OpenEval R9 addresses face-name association specificity (C96-C101, C44, C46, C98-C99) with detailed analysis showing smaller effects and cognitive psychology interpretation. No corresponding peer review evaluation found addressing this specific pattern of results.

OpenEval R11 specifically validates spatial specificity through control region analysis (C88-C89) beyond what peer reviewers explicitly addressed. While peer reviewers praised overall methodology, they did not specifically comment on the control region findings.

OpenEval R13 provides extensive validation of biophysical modeling and mechanistic hypothesis (C116-C131) including electric field modeling showing tACS alone insufficient. While peer reviewers accepted the general mechanism, they did not specifically address the detailed biophysical modeling claims.

OpenEval R15 addresses future research recommendations (C142-C144) as logical extensions. No corresponding peer review evaluation found specifically addressing these forward-looking methodological suggestions.

OpenEval R17 validates extensive background and literature context (C1-C2, C12-C31) as appropriately supported by citations. Peer reviewers did not specifically evaluate these background claims, focusing instead on methods and findings.

OpenEval R18 addresses broad interpretive synthesis (C86-C87, C90-C92, C103-C105, C108-C113) integrating findings with literature. While peer reviewers accepted individual findings, they did not provide specific evaluation of these synthetic interpretive claims beyond general acceptance.
